newsitem.title: USA: New Orleans revelers chant Mardi Gras mantra.
newsitem.headline: New Orleans revelers chant Mardi Gras mantra.

text.p: Shivering in near freezing temperatures, thousands of revellers huddled together on Tuesday chanting the mantra of Mardi Gras -- "Throw me something, mister!" -- as gaudy floats with trinket-tossing masked riders inched through the city's packed streets.

The last day of debauchery before the Christian Lent begins on Ash Wednesday kicked off about 7:30 a.m. (1230 GMT) with walking groups, including famed Dixieland clarinetist Pete Fountain's Half-Fast Marching Club, strolling through the crowds and making bar stops along the parade route.

The non-stop parades began in earnest in the city when the Krewe of Zulu, a predominantly African-American Carnival club, rolled down St. Charles Avenue toward the French Quarter handing out hand-painted coconuts along with the obligatory rubber spears and reams of plastic beads.

But Mardi Gras celebrations were not limited to New Orleans and its suburbs. Parades rolled across south Louisiana from the cities of Lafayette and Lake Charles to tiny waterfront communities like Lafitte, where decorated shrimp boats and pirogues drifted down the bayous.

In the towns of Mamou and Eunice, Cajun traditions prevailed in the Courir de Mardi Gras as masked and costumed horseback riders scoured the countryside for live chickens, okra, rice and sausage for community cauldrons of gumbo and a street dance.

Law enforcement officers across the state reported no serious crimes or incidents involving revellers. "We've got the usual number of arrests of drunks who get too belligerant or dope-smokers who insist on blowing the stuff in our faces," one New Orleans officer said. "But it's really very hard to get arrested on Mardi Gras down here. You have to work at it."
Near the French Quarter, two shivering young men were dressed in identical leather G-strings, a few chains and elaborately feathered masks.
"It's cold, but we get a little warmer with every beer," one said. "The trick is to stay in the middle of a crowd. It cuts the wind."
The more flamboyant and daring costumes were found closer to the Vieux Carre, while family themes and picnics prevailed away from the centre of town.

Many New Orleanians throw themselves whole-heartedly into the street party atmosphere year after year, returning to the same parade-watching spots and costuming every family member from grandmothers to infants.
"I wouldn't miss it for nothin', darlin," said Edith Danapales of suburban Chalmette as she flipped hamburgers on a portable grill on the St. Charles Avenue median.

"We've been doing this since my grandpa was knee-high to a crawfish," she said. "That's why we all dress like crawfish every year and just add new costumes for those who can't fit in last year's. I think there's 33 of us this year -- maybe 34."
By late afternoon, most of the parades were over, but the partying for die-hards normally goes on until midnight, when police clear the streets and garbage trucks move in.
"This is the world's biggest street party," said one New Orleans policeman. "It's a lot of work for us, but it's fun, it's free and even crime takes a holiday for Mardi Gras."
